transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-05
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Sai Patel (Redwood SE), Linda Park (Head of ML, Hearthline), Marcus Reed (CTO, Hearthline), Aisha Khan (Dev Lead, Hearthline)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics. Covered streaming responses, request parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry semantics and idempotency, and how the Redwood Console and Optimize recommendations can help manage cost/latency. Customer asked about data residency, SOC 2, VPC options, and dedicated vs hosted trade-offs. Agreed next steps: pricing comparision, benchmark spreadsheet, and POC scoping call.

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um i'm jordan from redwood, i'll keep this short, sai will do the demo — thanks for making time
00:07 Linda: thanks, yeah we wanna see how this would fit into our triage assistant project, we have some latency sensitive flows and also PHI concerns so, you know, security is top of mind
00:15 Sai: great — i'll share my screen in a sec, but quick agenda: hosted API basics for chat/text generation, streaming, params, retry behavior, plus quick look at the console and optimize suggestions
00:28 Marcus: quick question — are we assuming this is hosted or dedicated? we are evaluating both, cost/latency tradeoffs are key
00:35 Jordan: good call out. today's demo is hosted-first — show the API and console. we'll call out where dedicated or private would change things (SLA, VPC, unit cost)
00:45 Sai: okay sharing screen, pardon any small lag. so here's a simple chat request example — header for auth, model selection, messages array. we set temperature and top_p, you can see max_tokens and stop sequences
01:05 Sai: note on streaming — the API supports chunked streaming over server-sent events or websockets, depending on your client. streaming helps reduce perceived latency since tokens arrive as generated
01:18 Linda: do we get partial tokens billed? curious how billing works with streaming
01:22 Sai: billing is token-based — streaming is just delivery; cost is per token generated, same as non-streaming. one caveat: when you retry a streamed request you might need to dedupe by using an idempotency key so you don't double-bill for a partially-delivered response
01:37 Marcus: idempotency key? how does that work with long-running chats and reconnects
01:42 Sai: we recommend an idempotency key header on initial request; on reconnect the server will reconcile and either resume or return the completed generation if it's still available. retries follow exponential backoff; SDKs include helpers for safe retries
01:58 Sai: example params: temperature (0-1), top_p, top_k (if available for model), max_tokens. we also have presence/ frequency penalties in the model config. for chat specifically we pass role-labelled messages
02:15 Aisha: do you support function/tool calling? we have structured output mechanisms in our pipeline that expect JSON
02:20 Sai: yes — function calling is supported. you can define a function schema and the model will either call it or return structured JSON, then you can validate on your side. console shows traces of function calls so you can debug faster
02:35 Jordan: quick note on retries and quality — if you see flaky outputs on retries, our Optimize tool can suggest temperature and quantization adjustments and point to caching prefixes to reduce variability
02:48 Linda: can you show streaming in the console so we can see logs/traces?
02:52 Sai: sure — here is the request map. we show per-token latency, request timeline, model version, and token-level cost estimate. you can also set alerts for tail latency and token usage spikes
03:08 Marcus: what about prefix/KV cache? we have a heavyweight system prompt for clinical context that repeats a lot
03:13 Sai: good use case for KV cache or prefix caching — you can pin large static context to avoid re-sending it, that reduces tokens and cost. Optimize will detect stable prefixes and recommend caching policies
03:27 Sai: back to streaming: here's a demo — i'm sending a prompt and you can see the SSE chunks come in. there will be occasional mis-transcribed words in the console transcript because auto-transcription isn't perfect, but the raw response payload is preserved
03:45 Marcus: okay latency looked good in the demo, but what's your p50/p95 numbers for our average payload sizes — say 200 tokens per request
03:54 Sai: for hosted we publish model profiles — e.g., redwood-minerva-v1 (ex) p50 ~60ms per token on recent runs, p95 depends on concurrency; hosted p95 for 200 token flows typically under 1.2s but depends on batch sizing. Dedicated gives more predictable tail latency if you need hard SLOs
04:18 Linda: and encryption / data residency — how long is customer data retained? we need to know about logs and any persistence for PHI concerns
04:26 Jordan: security pack: hosted can be configured with strict retention policies and we offer SOC 2 Type II, and you can integrate with your KMS for envelope encryption. for PHI-heavy usage, we also offer Private deployments with VPCs or on-prem packages
04:43 Linda: do you have audit logs for prompts and responses? compliance needs that for incident investigations
04:48 Sai: yep audit logs and per-request metadata are available via the console, retention windows configurable as an add-on. we can exclude full-text logging if you want token-level anonymization
05:02 Aisha: about retries again — if we have 429s under burst, would you recommend client-side linear backoff or a specific retry policy?
05:10 Sai: exponential backoff with jitter is what we recommend; the SDK has a default policy tuned for our rate limits. for bursty production traffic we suggest a token-based quota and smoothing layer or use Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput
05:27 Marcus: how does the SDK handle streaming reconnects — is there built-in resume?
05:33 Sai: SDK includes helpers to reattach with the idempotency key and resume from last ack token in some cases; if you can't resume we recommend truncating partial tokens and re-requesting with prefix caching to avoid redundant context
05:48 Jordan: i'll mention pricing briefly — hosted is usage based per token; dedicated moves to reserved capacity model which can reduce unit cost but adds commit. we'll send a concise hosted vs dedicated comparison doc after the call
06:02 Linda: any guardrails for hallucinations? clinical correctness is essential for us
06:08 Sai: we recommend prompt engineering plus retrieval augmentation and model selection. Redwood Optimize can monitor quality drift on a set of eval prompts and send regression alerts. also reranking and grounding patterns help, and you can pin a smaller more deterministic model for critical paths
06:28 Aisha: do you support streaming partial JSON then finalizing? we need to stream partial structured responses to our downstream pipeline
06:34 Sai: yes — function calling with incremental outputs is supported by some of our model variants; we'll share examples. if streaming partial JSON is critical you should validate on the client side and have a reconciliation step on final chunk received
06:51 Marcus: who else from redwood would we talk to for a security deep dive?
06:55 Jordan: our security lead is available — i'll include them on the follow-up and share SOC 2 / ISO docs. we can also schedule a dedicated security review call
07:06 Linda: perfect. i also want to see latency numbers at our region — do you have per-region benchmarks?
07:12 Sai: yes we have region-specific profiles; we'll include a short benchmark sheet with p50/p95 numbers and sample token counts. you can also request a small dedicated pilot to test in your environment
07:25 Aisha: what's the typical onboarding time for an engineering team to go from sign-up to first production call?
07:31 Jordan: self-serve teams can be live in a day for basic flows; for secure enterprise setups with SSO, custom retention and private deploys expect 2-6 weeks depending on procurement
07:42 Sai: quick note on errors: 429s, 503s returned with structured error codes. we also emit request_id that maps into console traces so you can debug. the SDK surfaces retryable vs non-retryable codes
08:01 Jordan: ok let's run a small live example — sai, run a prompt that demonstrates streaming + retry behavior
08:08 Sai: sending prompt now... (streaming) - chunk 1... chunk 2.. oops small hiccup on my network, reconnecting — you see the client used the idempotency key and resumed, final chunk arrived
08:36 Linda: saw that, looks robust — good to know the SDK handles resume mostly transparently
08:42 Marcus: final question — what's the SLA on hosted?
08:46 Jordan: hosted has a best-effort SLA; Dedicated offers SLA-backed uptime and latency guarantees. for enterprises needing firm SLOs we usually recommend Dedicated + can optionally pair with Private for regulatory constraints
09:02 Sai: last bit — Optimize suggestions: auto-batching for similar sequence lengths, quantization profiles for cost savings, suggestions for model variants and cache settings. console shows a simulated cost impact before you flip any settings
09:20 Jordan: great. recap / next steps: we'll send pricing + hosted vs dedicated comparison, sai will share benchmark spreadsheet and sample prompts, jordan will loop in security and schedule a POC scoping call for 2026-05-12
09:34 Linda: thanks everyone — please include me and aisha on follow-up
09:38 Marcus: thanks, good demo
